lead: A requirement is a statement of what the software must do, or of how well it must do it. The two families fail in different ways: 'the app lists matching books' can be shown on a screen, while 'results arrive within 2 seconds' has to be measured with a stopwatch. Separating them tells the team what to build and what to test. Every project uses this split — a hospital booking screen, a UPI payment page, an IRCTC search — and every SRS is organised around it.
prereq: You need Unit 1 (what software is, and why projects fail); the requirement list is the first artifact a project produces.

blocks.text: A requirement is a capability or a condition that the delivered software must satisfy. Two families exist because the two kinds of statement are checked in different ways.

A functional requirement (FR) is a service the system provides: the input it accepts, the output it returns, and what happens when something goes wrong. 'A student searches the catalogue by title, author or ISBN and the app lists matching books' is functional. The 'no match found' message belongs to the same FR.

A non-functional requirement (NFR) is a quality or a restriction on those services — how fast, how safe, how easy. 'Search results appear within 2 seconds' is non-functional. Some syllabi call NFRs quality attributes; those that restrict the solution, such as a fixed phone model, are also called constraints.

blocks.text: A user requirement is written in natural language for the customer, with no design detail: 'The librarian marks a book as lost.' A system requirement expands it into something a developer can build and a tester can check: which field changes, which roles may trigger it, how the fine is computed, and which error appears when the book is already marked lost. One user requirement often becomes several system requirements.
Both levels sit in the SRS (see 2.5) and both are gathered by talking to stakeholders (see 2.3).

items: Performance: search answers in 2 s or less; 20 searches per second at peak.
Security: payment data travels over HTTPS.
Usability: a new student finds a book in 30 s without training.
Portability: runs on Android 8 and above.

blocks.text: An interface requirement fixes how this system talks to another: 'the app calls the payment gateway over its REST API, over HTTPS'. Only a few universities examine interface specification as a separate heading; elsewhere it is listed under system requirements or under NFRs.
An NFR needs a number, a condition and a unit, or it cannot be verified. 'The app must be user-friendly' fails; 'a new student finds a book in 30 seconds' passes.

figure.caption: Requirements split into a functional branch and a non-functional branch. Notice that performance, security and usability sit under non-functional, and that each branch starts as a user-level statement and is then expanded into system requirements.

spec.aria: A requirements tree whose root splits into a Functional branch (services, inputs and outputs, exceptions) and a Non-functional branch (performance, security, usability).

examples.question: A university library app has five statements. R1: a student searches the catalogue and sees matching books. R2: search results appear within 2 seconds. R3: the system stores 50,000 book records, each with 4 KB of metadata. R4: the app runs on Android 8 and above. R5: payments go to the gateway over HTTPS. (a) Classify R1 to R5. (b) Compute the catalogue metadata storage in MB, taking 1 MB = 1024 KB. (c) At peak, 20 searches arrive per second and each must finish in 2 s; how many searches are in progress at once?
steps: R1 is functional and sits at user level: a service described in the student's own words.
R2 is non-functional, performance: it constrains how well R1 runs, not what R1 does.
R3 is non-functional, capacity: it limits stored data. Storage = 50,000 records × 4 KB = 200,000 KB.
Convert: 200,000 KB ÷ 1024 KB per MB = 195.3125 MB, about 195.31 MB.
R4 is non-functional, a portability or platform constraint. R5 is an interface requirement that also carries a security constraint (HTTPS).
Searches in progress = arrival rate × time per search = 20 per second × 2 s = 40 searches.
examples.answer: R1 functional; R2 performance; R3 capacity; R4 platform constraint; R5 interface with a security constraint. Storage is 195.3125 MB (about 195.31 MB) and 40 searches are in progress at peak.

traps: Calling 'results within 2 seconds' a functional requirement. It says how well search works, so it is a non-functional performance requirement.
Writing a design choice as a requirement: 'use MySQL' or 'use a hash table' describes the solution. State the need, and record a mandated technology as a constraint.
Leaving an NFR without a number. 'Fast', 'secure' and 'user-friendly' cannot be verified; give a threshold, a condition and a unit.
Mistaking capacity for function. 'Stores 50,000 records' is a limit on the system, not a service it offers.
Mixing levels. 'The student searches the catalogue' is a user requirement; the field list, sort order and error codes behind it are system requirements.

quiz.q: Define functional requirement and non-functional requirement in one line each.
quiz.a: Functional: a service the system provides, with its inputs, outputs and exceptions. Non-functional: a quality or restriction on those services, such as performance, security, usability, reliability or capacity.

quiz.q: How does a user requirement differ from a system requirement?
quiz.a: A user requirement is a natural-language statement for the customer with no design detail. A system requirement expands it into the detail a developer builds and a tester checks; one user requirement often becomes several system requirements.

quiz.q: Why is 'the app must be user-friendly' a poor NFR? Rewrite it.
quiz.a: It has no number, no condition and no unit, so nothing can be measured or accepted. Rewrite: a new student finds a book in 30 seconds without training.

quiz.q: Classify: 'After login the app sends a one-time password by SMS within 10 seconds.'
quiz.a: Two requirements in one sentence: functional (send an OTP by SMS when login occurs) and non-functional performance (the OTP reaches the user within 10 s).

quiz.q: A system stores 20,000 records at 3 KB each. Compute the storage in MB using 1 MB = 1024 KB.
quiz.a: 20,000 × 3 KB = 60,000 KB; 60,000 ÷ 1024 = 58.59 MB. This is a non-functional capacity requirement.

quiz.q: A team writes 'use MySQL' and 'search returns in 2 s' on the requirement list. Which is wrong, and why?
quiz.a: 'Use MySQL' is a design decision, not a need, so it does not belong on the requirement list unless the client mandates that database, in which case it is recorded as a constraint. 'Search returns in 2 s' is a valid measurable NFR because it states a threshold and a unit.

quiz.q: Why keep functional and non-functional requirements apart when planning tests?
quiz.a: Functional requirements are verified by functional tests — use cases, equivalence partitioning, boundary values (see Unit 4, Software Testing Strategies and Techniques). Non-functional requirements are verified by performance, load, security, usability and configuration tests against measured thresholds. Keeping them apart makes each traceable to its own test type and stops a quality target from being lost among behaviour statements.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry an NFR is written as a quality-attribute scenario: a stimulus, a response, and a measured response. The ISO/IEC 25010 model groups product quality into characteristics such as performance efficiency, security and maintainability. Agile teams keep NFRs as acceptance criteria and performance budgets in the backlog, and architecture teams guard them with automated checks called fitness functions. Search 'quality attribute scenario', 'ISO 25010' and 'non-functional requirements backlog'.
